After: E is gone, shown dashed; its edges to D and F now attach to B, and the contracted edge itself has become a self-loop on B, all in the accent color." width="100%"} Given an edge between `node_1` and `node_2`, creates a new graph where `node_2` is merged into `node_1`. This is equivalent to `contract_nodes(node_1, node_2)` but explicitly requires that an edge exists between the nodes. Edge contraction shrinks a graph by one node while keeping its connectivity: every edge that touched `node_2` is re-attached to `node_1`, and `node_2` disappears. It is a basic operation in graph theory (graph minors, Karger's minimum-cut algorithm) and a practical way to simplify networks, for example: - merging two adjacent stops, junctions, or routers that should be treated as one - collapsing a duplicated entity (e.g., two records for the same person) that is linked by an edge - coarsening a graph step by step for multilevel layout or partitioning After the merge, edges at `node_1` that would now connect the same pair of nodes are collapsed into one (the first one found keeps its weight and attributes), so `node_1` has at most one edge to each neighbor and at most one self-loop. Edges between other nodes, parallel ones included, are kept as they are. The remaining nodes keep their IDs, labels and attributes, and surviving edges keep their IDs. The original graph is not modified. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node_1]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Source endpoint of the edge (node ID or label). This node survives the contraction and inherits all of `node_2`'s edges. [node_2]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int | str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Target endpoint of the edge (node ID or label). This node will be removed. In an undirected graph the order of `node_1` and `node_2` only decides which node survives. In a directed graph an edge from `node_1` to `node_2` must exist; an edge in the opposite direction does not qualify. [self_loops]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (default), the contracted edge becomes a self-loop on `node_1`. If `False`, the contracted edge is removed. Use `False` when self-loops would distort later analysis (e.g., degree counts or algorithms that do not accept them). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A new graph with the edge contracted. It has one node fewer than the original. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If no edge exists from `node_1` to `node_2` (including when either ID is not in the graph), if a label is not found, or if `node_1` and `node_2` are the same node. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Convenience wrapper around `contract_nodes(node_1, node_2)` that first checks an edge $(u, v)$ actually exists and raises `ValueError` if not. The distinction matters: `contract_nodes()` happily merges any two nodes, while `contracted_edge()` is the operation graph theorists usually mean when they talk about contracting *an edge*, so the guard rules out accidental merges of non-adjacent nodes. On undirected graphs edge orientation is irrelevant; on directed graphs the edge must point from $u$ to $v$, so contracting along a $(v, u)$ edge requires swapping the arguments (which also swaps which node survives). ## Examples {.doc-examples} Contracting the edge "A"-"B" in a three-node path leaves two nodes: ::: {#8c26fbda .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ( ec.Graph(directed=False) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) result = g.contracted_edge("A", "B") result.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: "B"'s other connections carry over to "A", so the former `B-C` edge now appears as `A-C`. The contracted edge itself survives as a self-loop on "A": ::: {#b8e7a1ad .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['A--A', 'A--C'] ``` ::: ::: With `self_loops=False`, the contracted edge is dropped instead: ::: {#c909efaa .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g.contracted_edge("A", "B", self_loops=False).get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['A--C'] ``` ::: ::: The same works on directed graphs -- contracting `A->B` redirects `B`'s outgoing edges to originate from `A` instead: ::: {#fa90f31f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) result = g.contracted_edge("A", "B") result.has_edge("A", "C") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: ::: On a directed graph the edge has to exist in the stated direction, so asking to contract "B" -> "A" here raises an error: ::: {#fb790837 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} try: g.contracted_edge("B", "A") except ValueError as e: print(e) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Edge (2, 1) does not exist in the graph ``` ::: :::
